blocks.text: Reading a definition of MCP is one thing, watching an actual conversation happen between a host and a server is another, and it is usually the moment the whole idea clicks. This lesson walks through one complete MCP session from the very first byte sent over the wire to the very last one, in order, so you can see exactly what happens at each step and why. Nothing here is abstract, every step includes the literal shape of the message that goes back and forth.
1. Step One: Opening a Connection

blocks.alt: A client opens a connection to the server
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439736195-924104776.png
Before any MCP message can be exchanged, the client and server first need a transport, a raw channel capable of carrying bytes back and forth.
As covered in MCP Architecture, this is commonly standard input and output for a server running as a local subprocess, or an HTTP-based streaming connection for a server running remotely.
Opening the connection itself is not yet part of the MCP protocol, it is just plumbing, a process gets spawned, or a socket gets opened, or an HTTP connection gets established.

At this point, nothing MCP-specific has happened yet. Neither side knows anything about the other, not its capabilities, not its version, not what it offers. The transport is simply live and ready to carry messages. Everything that gives the connection meaning happens in the very next step, initialization.

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: A live transport and an initialized MCP session are two different things. A process can be running and piping bytes correctly while the MCP handshake still has not happened.

blocks.text: 1.1 Stdio Versus Network Transports

A local stdio transport is the simplest possible case, the host spawns a child process and pipes its standard input and output directly, no networking stack involved at all. A remote transport instead relies on an HTTP connection that supports streaming in both directions, useful when the server lives on another machine entirely, perhaps a shared team server several people connect to at once.

blocks.text: 2. Step Two: The Initialize Request

blocks.alt: A client sends an initialize request to the server
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439736195-395390373.png

The client always speaks first. It sends an initialize request, a JSON-RPC call that announces the protocol version it supports, its own capabilities, and some basic information about the client implementation. This is the client formally introducing itself before asking the server for anything.

Notice the request carries an id, the value 1 in this case. Every JSON-RPC request that expects a reply carries an id, and the response that eventually comes back will echo that same id, which is how a client matches replies to the requests that triggered them when several calls might be in flight.
3. Step Three: The Initialize Response and Capability Exchange

The server answers with its own protocolVersion, its own capabilities, and some serverInfo. This is the moment both sides agree on what is actually available for the rest of the session, if the client asked about a capability the server does not support, the server simply omits it from its reply rather than erroring out.

Both sides now know the protocol version in use and exactly which categories of features, tools, resources, prompts, are on the table for this particular server. A client should never assume a server offers something it did not explicitly declare here.
3.1 What Happens on a Version Mismatch

If the client requests a protocol version the server does not understand, the server is expected to respond with the closest version it does support rather than simply failing, giving the client a chance to decide whether it can still proceed. In practice, well-maintained clients and servers converge on the same handful of protocol versions quickly, so a mismatch is rare, but it is exactly the kind of edge case worth testing deliberately when building your own client.
4. Step Four: The Initialized Notification

After receiving the initialize response, the client sends one more message, a notifications/initialized notification, confirming it has processed the handshake and is ready to proceed. This is a notification, not a request, which means it carries no id and expects no reply.

This small message matters more than it looks. Until the server receives it, some implementations will refuse to accept any further calls, since the handshake is not considered fully closed out from the client side until this confirmation arrives. Only after this point does the session count as genuinely open for normal use.
5. Step Five: Discovering Tools

blocks.alt: A client lists tools to get available tools
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439736196-664731400.png

With the session open, the client typically asks the server what it can actually do. A tools/list request returns every tool the server currently exposes, along with a name, a description, and a JSON Schema describing its expected input, exactly the kind of machine-readable schema discussed in earlier lessons on why MCP matters.
The server responds with a list, here shortened to a single entry for clarity, but a real server might expose a dozen or more tools in one response.
5.1 Why Discovery Happens Before Any Tool Runs

Discovery exists specifically so the model never has to guess what a server can do. Compare this to a hand-written integration where a developer reads documentation once, months earlier, and hardcodes the available calls, if the server changes what it offers, that hardcoded list silently goes stale. MCP discovery instead happens fresh at the start of a session, every single time, so the model always sees the server current, real, current set of tools.

blocks.title: Refreshing mid-session
blocks.content: If a server's tools change while a session is already open, it can send a notifications/tools/list_changed notification, prompting the client to call tools/list again rather than waiting for the next fresh connection.

blocks.text: 6. Step Six: Discovering Resources

Separately, a resources/list request asks what read-only, addressable data the server can hand over, files, database rows, cached documents, anything with a stable identifier the host might want to pull into context. Resources are described by a uri, a name, and usually a mimeType.

Not every server exposes resources, some are tool-only. That is exactly why the capability exchange in step three matters, a client that never received a resources capability from the server should not bother sending this request at all, since it already knows the answer will be empty or unsupported.
7. Step Seven: Discovering Prompts

A prompts/list request asks for reusable, pre-written prompt templates the server ships with, often parameterized snippets that encode a good way of asking for something this particular server is good at. These are less commonly used than tools and resources, but they follow the identical list-then-use shape.

blocks.text: 8. Step Eight: The Model Chooses a Tool to Call
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439736196-790696266.png

Discovery results, tool names, descriptions, and schemas, get folded into what the underlying AI model sees, typically as part of its system context or its available function list. From there, the decision to actually use a tool is made by the model itself, based on the user's request, exactly the same way a model decides whether to call any function in ordinary function calling.

MCP has nothing to do with how the model decides, it only standardizes what happens once that decision has been made and needs to be executed against a real server. This distinction, the model deciding versus MCP executing, is explored in full depth in the later lesson comparing MCP against function calling.
9. Step Nine: Sending the Tool Call Request

blocks.alt: A client sends a tool call request to the server
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439736197-528332818.png

Once a tool and its arguments are chosen, the client sends a tools/call request naming the tool and supplying arguments that must satisfy the inputSchema advertised during discovery. This is the one message in the whole session that actually causes something to happen in the outside world, everything before it was just introductions.
The id here, 5, is new and unrelated to the ids used during discovery, each JSON-RPC request on a connection gets its own id, generated by whichever side initiated that particular call.
9.1 Validating Arguments Before Sending

A well-behaved client validates its arguments against the tool's inputSchema locally before ever sending the tools/call request, catching an obviously malformed call, a missing required field, a string where a number was expected, without spending a round trip to the server just to hear about it. This is the same JSON Schema validation pattern used across most modern API tooling, nothing MCP-specific about the validation step itself.
10. Step Ten: The Server Executes and Returns a Result

blocks.alt: A server executes and produces a result
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439736197-82632583.png

The server does the actual work, opening the file, hitting a database, calling a third-party API, whatever the tool is implemented to do, and returns the outcome as content inside its response. Content is typically returned as one or more typed content blocks, most often plain text, so the model can read it directly.

That result flows back through the client, into the host, and into the model's context, at which point the model can read the file contents as if they had simply appeared in the conversation, and continue reasoning about the user's original question.
11. Step Eleven: Handling an Error Case

Not every tool call succeeds. Suppose the same read_file call is made against a path that does not exist. The server does not crash the connection or send back a malformed message, it returns a normal, well-formed result with isError set to true and an explanatory message inside content.

This is a deliberate design choice covered in Problems Solved by MCP: tool-level failures are reported inside a normal result so the model can read the error message and decide what to do next, retry with a different path, ask the user for clarification, or try a different tool entirely. A hard JSON-RPC protocol-level error, by contrast, is reserved for something more fundamental, like calling a tool name that does not exist at all.

items: A tool-level error: the tool ran, but the operation failed, reported via isError inside a normal result.
A protocol-level error: the request itself was invalid, reported via the JSON-RPC error field instead of result.

blocks.text: 11.1 Common JSON-RPC Error Codes

blocks.content: {"headers":["Code","Meaning"],"rows":[["-32700","Parse error, the message was not valid JSON"],["-32600","Invalid request, the message did not match the expected shape"],["-32601","Method not found, an unknown method name was called"],["-32602","Invalid params, the arguments did not match what the method expects"]]}

blocks.text: These codes come directly from the underlying JSON-RPC 2.0 specification that MCP builds on, they are not MCP inventions. Recognizing them is useful the moment you start writing your own client, since a bug in your request formatting will usually surface as one of exactly these four codes.
12. Step Twelve: Notifications During a Long-Running Call

Some tool calls take a while, a large search, a slow external API, a multi-step operation. While such a call is in flight, a server can send progress notifications back to the client, giving the host a chance to show a progress indicator instead of leaving the user staring at a frozen screen.

Notifications never carry an id and never receive a direct reply, they are one-way information, separate from the request-response pair that eventually delivers the actual result once the work finishes.
13. Step Thirteen: Closing the Session
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439736198-3107497.png

Eventually the conversation ends, the user closes the host application, or the host decides it no longer needs that particular server for now. Closing a session is mostly a transport-level concern: for a subprocess-based server, the client stops the process; for a network connection, the connection is closed cleanly.

There is no elaborate MCP-level goodbye handshake required, the emphasis in MCP has always been on a clean, simple initialize at the start, everything after that is ordinary requests, responses, and notifications until the transport itself goes away. Well-behaved servers release any resources tied to that session, open file handles, database connections, cached state, as soon as they detect the connection has ended.
13.1 Timeouts as a Practical Safety Net

Real clients almost always wrap each outstanding request in a timeout, a tool call that never responds within a reasonable window is treated as failed rather than left hanging forever, and the session can then either retry or be torn down cleanly. MCP itself does not mandate a specific timeout value, that is left to the client implementation to decide based on what makes sense for its users.
14. A Worked Example: One Full Conversation, Start to Finish
Picture a user typing "summarize the Q3 report" into a host application connected to a file-system server. Here is the entire sequence, condensed into the order the messages actually travel.

items: 1. Transport opens, the server process starts.
2. Client sends initialize, server replies with its capabilities.
4. Client sends tools/list, learns about read_file.
5. The model decides it needs the file, the client sends tools/call for read_file.
6. Server reads the file, returns its text content.
7. The model reads that content and produces a summary for the user.
8. The user closes the app, the transport closes.

blocks.title: The one line that matters most
blocks.content: Every one of those eight steps is a plain JSON-RPC message, there is no hidden magic anywhere in this list, just requests, responses, and one notification, in a fixed, predictable order.

blocks.text: 15. Common Mistakes When Implementing an MCP Workflow

items: Calling tools/list or tools/call before the initialize handshake has finished, some servers will reject this outright.
Forgetting to send notifications/initialized and wondering why the server behaves as if the session never fully started.
Treating a tool-level isError result as if the whole connection had failed, and tearing down the session instead of just letting the model see the error.
Assuming every server supports resources or prompts, without checking the capabilities returned in the initialize response first.
Reusing the same JSON-RPC id for a new request while an earlier one with that id is still outstanding, which makes it impossible to match responses correctly.
Not handling progress notifications at all, leaving users staring at an unresponsive screen during a slow tool call.

blocks.text: 16. Practice: Trace Your Own Tool Call

Pick any single tool from a server you are familiar with, even a hypothetical one, a weather lookup, a database query, a calendar check. Write out, in order, the exact JSON-RPC messages that would need to travel across the wire to go from a cold connection to receiving that tool's result. Do not skip the handshake steps, they are the part beginners most often forget to include.

code.content:
# Fill in each step for your own tool, following the pattern from this lesson
# 1. initialize request  ->
# 2. initialize response <-
# 3. initialized notification ->
# 4. tools/list request ->
# 5. tools/list response <-
# 6. tools/call request ->
# 7. tools/call response <-

blocks.text: Then write the same trace again, but this time assume step 6 fails, your tool cannot find what it was asked for. What does the response at step 7 look like, and what should the model do next with that information.
Key Takeaway

An MCP conversation is not mysterious once you see the actual messages: connect, initialize, confirm, discover tools and resources and prompts, call a tool, receive a result or a clearly marked error, and eventually close the transport, all of it plain JSON-RPC requests, responses, and notifications in a fixed order.

This step-by-step walkthrough is the procedural companion to MCP Architecture, the next lesson, MCP Terminology, now locks down the precise vocabulary for every term used loosely in this walkthrough, host, client, server, capability, session, transport, and the rest, so there is no ambiguity left in any of it.
